title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This consolidated playbook describes the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, operational runbooks for common incidents, release notes process, and team wiki links. It is intended for engineers and SREs who operate and evolve the Redwood Inference serving runtime (services: serving-runtime-api, kernel-selector, scheduler, kv-cache-daemon, profiling-agent, benchmark-runner).

Goals and audience:
- Provide a single reference for architecture and operational guidance.
- Surface concrete SLOs, thresholds, and ownership.
- Document repeatable profiling and benchmarking steps used for performance regressions and model onboarding.
- Capture known issues and mitigations to shorten incident TTR.

1) High-level architecture (overview)
- Components:
  - serving-runtime-api: gRPC/REST front-end that validates requests, enforces routing policies, and forwards to the scheduler.
  - scheduler: request router & load balancer. Enforces latency SLO routing, batching windows, and capacity policies.
  - kernel-selector: chooses optimal kernel variant (fp16/fp32/quantized), CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels or CPU fallbacks, and manages per-model kernel policy.
  - kv-cache-daemon: long-lived KV cache for prefix caching and fast KV retrieval across requests.
  - profiling-agent: lightweight agent that captures per-batch timelines, CUDA timelines, and kernel counters.
  - benchmark-runner (repo: infra/serving/benchmarks): benchmarking harness used in CI and release validation.

- Dataflow (short): request -> serving-runtime-api -> scheduler (batching) -> kernel-selector -> device execution -> kv-cache (optional) -> streaming response.

- SLOs and targets:
  - Availability: 99.95% per-region for serving-runtime-api (excl. maintenance windows).
  - Latency targets (observed under normal traffic):
    - Small models (<= 3B): p50 < 20ms, p95 < 60ms, p99 < 120ms.
    - Medium models (3B-13B): p50 < 40ms, p95 < 150ms, p99 < 300ms.
    - Large models (>= 70B): throughput-focused; target p95 < 1s for streaming-first responses.
  - Error budget: 0.05% monthly for API errors (5xx), tracked by eng-sre.

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies
- Objectives:
  - Maximize device utilization while meeting per-request latency SLOs.
  - Allow graceful degradation via kernel fallbacks and model-variant routing.

- Scheduling primitives and policies:
  - Preemptive batch scheduling: small low-latency requests are prioritized with short batching windows (default 5ms for latency-tier L0). Throughput tiers (L1/L2) use longer windows (20-50ms).
  - GPU affinity: workloads are colocated by model family and memory footprint; large KV-cache warm models pinned to dedicated GPUs to minimize eviction thrash.
  - CUDA stream partitioning: each scheduler slot gets dedicated CUDA streams; kernels that support concurrent kernels are profiled and classified as 'concurrent-friendly'.
  - Kernel selection rules (kernel-selector):
    1. If model has quantized profile for current hardware and quantization-safety flag true -> prefer quantized kernel.
    2. Else if fp16 kernels meet accuracy gates -> prefer fp16.
    3. Else fall back to fp32.
  - Fallback and compatibility matrix: kernel-selector maintains a compatibility table per model-version -> device-type -> kernel-variant. When capacity constrained, scheduler can route to compatible model variants (smaller model or different quantization) using automatic fallback policy.

- Configurable knobs (examples):
  - batching_window_ms: 5 | 10 | 20 | 50
  - preempt_threshold_percent: 60 (if execution queue > 60% full, preempt throughput tasks)
  - kernel_concurrency_limit: 4 (max concurrent kernels per GPU multiprocessor for mixed workloads)

3) Profiling playbook (when to run + steps)
- When to profile:
  - Regressions in p95/p99 latency after a release.
  - New model onboarding or quantization profile changes.
  - Repeated OOMs or CUDA timeouts.

- Quick capture (5-10 minutes):
  1. Enable short-term profiler on target nodes: sudo systemctl start profiling-agent@NODE_ID
  2. Collect a 5-minute trace: profiling-agent collect --target serving-runtime-api --duration 300 --out /tmp/trace.tar.gz
  3. Run local trace analysis: profiling-agent analyze /tmp/trace.tar.gz --summary > /tmp/trace-summary.txt
  4. Upload artifact to S3: aws s3 cp /tmp/trace.tar.gz s3://redwood-inference/perf-traces/$(date +%Y%m%d)-NODE_ID-trace.tar.gz
  5. Link trace in the incident ticket and notify eng-serving-runtime on Slack (#serving-runtime).

- Deep profiling (for regressions):
  - Collect CUDA timelines (nvprof/nvtx) on a canary node with representative load. Use device metrics: sm_efficiency, dram_util, shared_util; and kernel durations.
  - GPU-level counters via nsight (if available) or nvidia-smi dmon for memory bandwidth.
  - Example capture script:
```
# run on canary node
export DURATION=600
profiling-agent collect --target scheduler --duration $DURATION --cuda-timeline --counters sm_efficiency,dram_util,shared_util --out /tmp/deep-trace.tar.gz
```

- Analysis checklist:
  - Are slow requests concentrated in one model-version or across multiple?
  - Is kernel runtime dominated by a single kernel (matmul/attention) or memory stalls?
  - Is there increased CPU-to-GPU transfer time? (look for memcpy H2D/D2H spikes)
  - Did kernel-selector choose a different variant after the release?

4) Benchmarking suite (CI + release validation)
- Location: infra/serving/benchmarks
- Core scripts: run_bench.py, compare_results.py, fixtures/:
  - config.yaml example:
```
workload:
  model: redwood-13b-v2
  seq_len: 512
  batch_sizes: [1,4,8,16]
  modes: [latency, throughput]
hardware:
  target: g4dn.12xlarge
  devices: [A100-80GB]
```
- Bench categories:
  - Latency microbenchmarks (single request, warm/unwarm, p50/p95/p99).
  - Throughput sweeps (saturate GPUs, measure tokens/sec, memory footprint).
  - Mixed workload simulation (mix of L0 latency-critical and L2 throughput requests).
- CI gating rules:
  - All serving runtime releases must pass the benchmark smoke suite on master: max_regression_vs_baseline p95 <= +10% else block.
  - Full validation for release-candidate on dedicated hardware (release lab) with baselines recorded in performance-metrics bucket.

5) Release notes and rollout procedure
- Versioning: YYYY.MM.DD[-RC#] for internal releases; public releases mapped to semver.
- Release checklist for runtime components:
  1. Build and unit tests (CI).
  2. Functional integration tests: small model + chat flow.
  3. Benchmark smoke: run_bench.py --smoke. Compare to baseline.
  4. Canary rollout (10% traffic) for 2h, monitor p95/p99, error rate, GPU memory utilization.
  5. Gradual ramp (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 30-60m observation windows.
- Rollback criteria (immediate rollback if any triggers):
  - p99 latency increases by > 2x vs baseline in canary window.
  - Error rate (5xx) > 0.25% absolute increase.
  - Sustained GPU OOMs on >= 2 nodes.

6) Runbooks (common incidents)
- Incident: p99 latency spike for small models
  1. Check recent deploys (k8s deployments, kernel-selector config changes).
  2. Pull metrics: p99 latency by model-version, scheduler queue length, batching_window_ms, CUDA SM utilization.
  3. If queue length high and preempt_threshold reached: reduce batching_window_ms for L0 to 2ms and increase preempt_threshold_percent to 80% temporarily.
  4. If kernel-selector recently switched to fp32: set model rollout to previous kernel_variant and trigger canary rollback.
  5. Collect profile trace (see profiling playbook) and assign to runtime perf-owner.
  6. Document mitigation and follow-up bug in backlog.

- Incident: GPU OOMs
  1. Identify affected pods: kubectl get pods -o wide | grep OOMKilled.
  2. Evacuate node: cordon + drain non-critical pods.
  3. Reduce per-slot max_batch_size and temporarily disable large-batch scheduling.
  4. If repeated OOM on same node type -> mark node type as tainted in scheduler until fix.
  5. Open a ticket with eng-infra for capacity and node failure analysis.

- Incident: Kernel fallback thrash / increased error rate
  1. Check kernel-selector logs for compatibility failures.
  2. If misclassification: add rule to compatibility table and restart kernel-selector on canary first.
  3. If widespread, route traffic to safe model variant using routing policy: curl -X POST https://admin-api/route/set -d '{"model":"redwood-13b-v1","traffic":100}'

7) Known issues (active/tracked)
- ISSUE-2027-01: Intermittent nvlink stalls on A100-80GB causing p99 spikes for large-attn models. Mitigation: pin large-attn models to single GPU until a firmware fix. (Owner: hw-platform)
- ISSUE-2026-12: Profiling-agent version 0.9.1 drops nsight counters under heavy load; upgraded agent 0.9.3 required. (Workaround: use low overhead sampling)
- ISSUE-2026-11: kernel-selector sometimes prefers fp16 even when accuracy gate fails for certain token lengths. Fix in progress (PR #432).

8) Team wiki and onboarding pointers
- Quickstart for new SREs:
  - Read: serving-runtime-reference-2026-03-04.json and this playbook.
  - Local dev: repo infra/serving, run: make dev-scheduler and dev-api.
  - Useful dashboards: Dashboards -> Serving Runtime -> p99 by model, Scheduler -> queue_length, Hardware -> GPU memory utilization.
  - Slack channels: #serving-runtime (ops), #serving-perf (benchmarks), #serving-kernel (kernel selector).

9) Ownership and contacts
- Runtime architecture & kernel scheduling: Marcus Lee (serving-runtime team).
- Profiling & benchmarks: Sofia Ramirez (perf team).
- SRE oncall (incidents): eng-sre rota; primary contact: oncall+serving@redwood.ai.

10) Appendices
- Example kernel-selector config (YAML):
```
kernel_selector:
  policies:
    - name: latency-first
      batching_window_ms: 5
      preferred_variants: [quantized, fp16, fp32]
    - name: throughput-first
      batching_window_ms: 40
      preferred_variants: [fp16, quantized, fp32]
```
- Helpful commands:
  - Check scheduler queues: kubectl exec -it scheduler-0 -- /bin/sh -c "curl localhost:8080/metrics | grep queue_length"
  - Force canary rollback: curl -X POST https://admin-api/rollout/rollback -d '{"component":"kernel-selector","to":"2027.02.01"}'

If you have questions or need access to the benchmark lab or perf traces bucket, contact Sofia Ramirez or open an internal support ticket via the infra-support queue.
